content:
Below is a concise, 20-minute script you can use with slides or handouts. It has:
- A 5-minute introduction/why it matters  
- A 10-minute “How phishing works” demo + real world examples  
- A 5-minute “What to do if you see one” checklist  

Feel free to adapt length; add or trim slides depending on how much you want to demo live vs hand out printed cheat-sheets.

────────────────────────  
Slide 1 – **Header**  
“Protecting Our Firm: Spotting Phishing in 20 Minutes”  
“Your workstation is often the cheapest, most convenient doorway attackers use to get into our network.”  

────────────────────────  
Slide 2 – **Scenario (Hook)**  
“Last week a colleague typed her password into a page that LOOKED like our parcel delivery portal—only the URL wasn’t ours, it was a fake site mimicking UPS or DHL.”  
✓ Show the fake URL in the presenter notes or a small screen snippet (e.g., “winterthur-architekten.ch-ups-login.com” vs real “ups.com”).  

────────────────────────  
Slide 3 – **What is phishing?**  
Phishing = fake message (email, SMS, Slack DM, chat bot, popup) that pretends to be trustworthy to steal credentials, install malware, or get you to send money. Attackers impersonate colleagues, banks, vendors, IT support—even tax authorities.  

────────────────────────  
Slide 4 – **The hook (lure)**  
Attackers use a mixture of urgency and familiarity:

* Urgency  
  * “Your account will be locked in 5 minutes unless you re-enter your password.”  
  * “Invoice payment failed – click to approve immediately.”  
* Familiarity  
  * “Dear Clemens, the CAD file you requested is attached.”  
  * “Your delivery notification: UPS tracking #1Z… Please print the label.”  

────────────────────────  
Slide 5 – **Real examples seen in Switzerland / architecture firms**  

1. Email purporting to be “IT-Helpdesk@winterthur-architekten.ch”  
   Subject: “Security Patch Required – Urgent”  
   Body:  
   > “Due to a security vulnerability detected, please update your login credentials by replying to this email or clicking the link below.”  
   → Red flags: vague sender domain (maybe winterthur–architekten.ch-helpdesk.info), links hidden behind “login.winterthur-architekten.ch-update” instead of “its.winterthur-architekten.ch”.

2. SMS from “Swiss Post / DHL” about “Your package requires customs clearance – pay CHF 12.90 here”  
   Short link: bit.ly/Zoll-Gebuehr  
   → Swiss tax or customs will never ask for payment via a short link.

3. Slack DM pretending to be “HR Lisa”:  
   > “Hi Clemens, latest payroll PDF attached. Let me know if anything changes ⤵”  
   Attachment is PDF with a macro or a fake sharepoint link (office365-login.winterthurfake.ch).

4. Popup from a PDF sent in an email (common in architecture):  
   “Adobe Reader needs to update – click Yes to continue.”  
   → Legitimate Adobe updaters install from adobe.com; fake popups often have typos or a different domain.

────────────────────────  
Slide 6 – **Key red-flag checklist (posterise or handout)**  

| Criterion | Example | What you do |
|-----------|---------|-------------|
| **Unexpected sender** | email from “HR Lisa <hr@winterthur-real.ch>” but the reply address is “hrsupport.winterthurfake.ch” | Hover mouse over the From line → check exact address |
| **Urgency / threats** | “Your account will be suspended in 10 minutes” | Pause → verify through other means (call helpdesk on known phone) |
| **Odd links** | tinyurl.com/archi-login | Hover or right-click → view full URL |  
| **Mismatched branding** | UPS logo but low resolution / off-color | Compare to official site |  
| **Requests personal data** | email asking for password, banking details | NEVER reply; delete immediately |
| **Attachment surprises** | “final blueprint.pdf” sent when you never asked | Confirm with sender via separate channel (phone call) |

────────────────────────  
Slide 7 – **Technical deep-dive on fake links (5 min)**  

1. **URL of fake login page:**  
   https://its.winterthur-architekten.ch-login-update.info  
   vs legit: https://its.winterthur-architekten.ch

2. **DNS & certificate quirks:**  
   • Some fake pages use HTTPS but the cert name matches a generic or invalid domain (“winterthur-architekten.ch” on the cert but the certificate is issued to “fake.dyndns.org”).  
   • Expired cert warnings = possible phish.

3. **Hover tips:**  
   Show live demo—open a browser and type “fake link” → you’ll see the destination URL pops up.  
   Practice together in the room: open any email in the inbox → hover over every hyperlink.

────────────────────────  
Slide 8 – **What if you think it’s real?**  

1. **Stop.** Do not click, do not reply.  
2. **Verify independently:**  
   • Call the sender at a known phone number (look it up from previous emails or the firm directory).  
   • Log into the service in a new browser tab (don’t click the link in the email).  
   • Ask a coworker “Did you expect this email?”  
3. **Report:**  
   – Forward the suspicious email to IT: phish@winterthur-architekten.ch  
   – Mark it as phishing in Outlook (Report -> Phishing).  
   – In Slack or Teams, use the /report or give channel moderators the link/msg.

────────────────────────  
Slide 9 – **Quick “Try-Before-Always” Drill (Live 3 min)**  

Ask one volunteer to open any recent email (from your own inbox, not private!).  
Together, hover over every link, check the exact domain, look for custom fonts or mismatched logos, and note any urgency words.  

Point out: if domain is merely “winterthur-architekten-login.com” → treat it as suspicious.

────────────────────────  
Slide 10 – **Policy summary**  

- Firm rule: NEVER share passwords, OTP codes, or client data via email, SMS, or unsolicited chat.  
- IT will never “ask” for passwords over email.  
- Multi-factor authentication (MFA) already enforced for Office 365 and Revit server login → phishers can’t access even if they get your password.

────────────────────────  
Slide 11 – **Take-Away Handout** (1-pager)

| Action | How | Real-life Swiss context |
|--------|-----|--------------------------|
| Hover before click | Right-click → “Copy link address” then paste in notepad | A “Swiss Post” link with .ch but extra subfolder |
| Verify sender | Type their real email (found in earlier correspondence) | Good practice when HR says “payroll attached” |
| Attachments only from known senders | Confirm by phone before opening | Many fake CAD/BIM files carry malware |
| Report anything doubtful | Forward to IT or click Outlook “Report Phishing” | Helps block repeat attacks for the whole firm |

────────────────────────  
Slide 12 – **Closing & Q&A**  

“Remember: The easiest phishing tool is simply a convincing subject line plus a familiar brand name. Being skeptical for sixty seconds often stops an attacker months of work inside our network.”

Open floor for questions, and offer a physical “Phishing Card” each employee can keep at their desk with the hover-and-check cheat-sheet printed on both sides.

Enjoy the session—and let’s keep Winterthur’s blueprints secure!
